title: The Endless Choir
premise: Edmund Almeida, a rationalist property surveyor, is hired to appraise the derelict Almeida family homestead and discovers a house that measures its occupants back — every photograph gains an extra chair, and the well on the property is slowly refilling with something that sings. The founders of the town built a ritual to keep the Choir fed, and Edmund's grandmother was the last keeper who abandoned it. To survive, Edmund must complete the interrupted ritual before the well brims over, but doing so means surrendering his memories of everyone he loves to become the Choir's new anchor. He finishes it, keeps one memory hidden in a photograph, and walks out hollow — belonging at last, at the price of everything that made him himself.
about_author: O. M. Okafor is a Nigerian-British writer of quiet horror whose stories explore inheritance, faith, and the architecture of grief. A former land surveyor, Okafor draws on years of measuring empty houses for a living.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. He arrives at the Almeida homestead with laser measures and skepticism, cataloguing decay for a bank file. The instruments return impossible readings — rooms larger inside than out. Emotional beat: smug competence beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Extra Seating
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Sorting his late grandmother's belongings, he notices every family photograph now contains one additional chair, always facing the camera. No one else sees it. Beat: creeping isolation as reality quietly edits itself around him.

chapters.title: The Well Register
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, with a found document excerpt. In the county archives he finds the homestead's water rights tied to a 'Choir Register' listing names ending with his grandmother's — and a blank line beneath. Beat: dread disguised as paperwork.

chapters.title: Neighborly Advice
chapters.summary: POV of Marisol Vann, elderly neighbor. She warns Edmund off the property, revealing her own sister 'joined' decades ago and still waves from an upstairs window that has no floor. Beat: first confirmation he isn't mad.

chapters.title: Measured Back
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Overnight, the survey data rewrites itself: the house now includes a room he never measured, furnished entirely with chairs. His tape measure hums when pointed at the well. Beat: the rationalist's tools betray him.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Hidden in the piano bench, grandma's ledger details the ritual: seven verses sung into the well each generation, memories offered as payment. Her final entry stops mid-verse. Beat: grief curdling into anger at her abandonment.

chapters.title: First Verse
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Desperate to stop the photographs multiplying chairs, he reads the opening verse aloud. The well answers in his grandmother's voice, one word off-key. Beat: terrible intimacy — the dead are listening.

chapters.title: The Congregation That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She attends a town meeting where no one will say the word 'Almeida'; the minutes show blank spaces where discussion should be. She realizes the town itself is complicit. Beat: communal guilt surfaces.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The well rises visibly overnight; wet footprints appear in dry halls. Photographs now show the chair occupied by a blurred figure wearing his coat. Beat: countdown pressure begins.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The house rearranges to trap him in the chair-room, where sitting feels like being remembered by something vast. He escapes through a window that shouldn't open. Beat: body horror of belonging.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She offers Edmund her sister's old notes on the ritual in exchange for a promise: if he survives, he'll sing her sister's name free. Beat: reluctant alliance, stakes made personal.

chapters.title: Second and Third Verses
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Singing deeper verses costs him small memories — his mother's laugh, a childhood street name. Each loss makes the house warmer, more welcoming. Beat: seduction of forgetting.

chapters.title: The Founders' Tape
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, intercut with 1912 transcript. A reel-to-reel recording reveals the founders didn't imprison the Choir — they invited it, trading remembrance for prosperity. Beat: the horror has a founding charter.

chapters.title: Drowned Hymnal
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Searching the flooded cellar, she recovers the hymnal but hears her sister singing below the waterline. She nearly joins her; Edmund pulls her out. Beat: the past actively recruits.

chapters.title: Half Empty, Half Him
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. He can no longer recall why he took this job, only that leaving feels unthinkable. The house has begun calling him 'keeper.' Beat: identity erosion reaches the point of no return.

chapters.title: Verse Six
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. One verse remains unfinished besides the last. Singing it floods him with borrowed memories — generations of keepers — and he understands the Choir isn't malevolent, only starving for witness. Beat: horrifying empathy.

chapters.title: Marisol's Name
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Edmund sings her sister free; the upstairs window goes dark, and Marisol weeps with relief and loss. But freeing a name weakens the seal — the well surges. Beat: mercy has a cost.

chapters.title: The Well Brims
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Water climbs the stairs singing in every voice he's lost. The final verse requires a keeper who chooses to stay. He sits in the extra chair. Beat: acceptance as climax threshold.

chapters.title: Last Verse
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, dissolving. He sings the seventh verse, offering his memories one by one — but palms a single photograph of his grandmother, tucking it against his heart where the Choir cannot count. Beat: sacrifice with one smuggled exception.

chapters.title: Keeper
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, fragmented. He becomes the anchor: warm, welcomed, belonging utterly, and unable to say what he paid. The house settles, satisfied. Beat: eerie peace after annihilation.

chapters.title: Closing the File
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Weeks later she files the appraisal herself, marking the property 'occupied.' In the final photograph, the chair faces away from the camera now — and someone has left flowers on it. Beat: mourning and complicity.

chapters.title: Appraised
chapters.summary: Epilogue, omniscient. A new surveyor arrives to appraise the homestead, finding one room too many and a ledger with a fresh name: Almeida, E., keeper. The well is quiet. For now. Beat: the cycle resumes, dread renewed.
